paper_title: DisaggKD: Efficient Knowledge Distillation through Teacher-Student Disaggregation and a Fused Loss

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Knowledge distillation (KD) frameworks place teacher and student on the same GPUs, so per-GPU memory limits the teachers that fit. DisaggKD separates them across nodes: teacher replicas stream hidden states to the student, a KD loss over row windows and vocabulary shards equals the full-vocabulary loss in exact arithmetic without forming the full-vocabulary logits, and a prefetch ring paces producer and trainer. Closed-form memory and traffic models locate the memory limits of each layout. On the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B to 9B pair, the disaggregated layout matches the LM loss of the colocated run with the same loss and is faster than that run; our fused loss also lets a colocated run train on as few nodes at faster speed, while the split is memory efficient when the student spans several nodes. On the larger pairs, colocated runs with a fused loss still run OOM where the split trains, because teacher weights and student states fill the budget.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Knowledge distillation (KD) trains student on its teachers output distribution (Hinton et al., 2015), and at pretraining scale SlimQwen uses it to recover the quality of compressed students (Tang et al., 2026). The 3 open frameworks we ran place the teacher on the students GPUs, keeping its weights beside the students weights, gradients, and optimizer state (NVIDIA, 2025a, 20242026) or offloading it between phases (NeMo RL, 2025; Zhang et al., 2026), as KDFlow optionally does. Colocated, the 2 models share 1 per-GPU memory budget, and the KD loss adds logits tensor over the full vocabulary for every token the student processes. That budget is the limit: with ModelOpts loss the colocated stack *Work was done during the internship at SB Intuitions Corp. 1 on the Qwen3.5 pair at 3 nodes runs out of memory (OOM) where the separated one fits (Figure 1), and our fused loss moves it but not the weights of larger teachers  (Table 3)  . We separate the 2 roles: the teacher runs forwardonly on its own nodes, so no GPU holds the layers of both models. The teacher sends its final hidden states, which are narrower than its vocabulary-wide logits, and the student recovers the logits with copy of the teachers output head. fused kernel then evaluates the KD loss over vocabulary shards from per-row statistics that combine across tensor-parallel (TP) ranks, without forming fullvocabulary tensor, so trainer memory stays low. Whether the split pays depends on per-GPU memory and on NVLink and InfiniBand traffic, so we derive closed-form estimates of both. Our contributions are: Estimation models (3) of per-GPU memory (3.1) and of traffic inside the student, inside the teacher, and between them (3.2), for both layouts (3.3); the memory model is fitted on measured peaks and OOM events, the traffic model checked against node counters (Appendices A.1, A.2). disaggregated KD algorithm, DisaggKD (4): teacher replicas stream hidden states over NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) point-to-point (P2P) links (4.1), the student evaluates fused loss over row windows and vocabulary shards, equal to the full-vocabulary loss in exact arithmetic (4.2, Appendix B.3), and prefetch ring paces both (4.3). measured evaluation (5). sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: KD for language models. At LLM scale the usual objective is the forward KL to the teachers next-token distribution, used alone or with hiddenstate losses in compression pipelines and model releases (Muralidharan et al., 2024; Bercovich et al., 2025; Gemma Team, 2024; NVIDIA, 2025c; Mistral Team, 2026) or studied as mixture with the LM loss (Tang et al., 2026; Peng et al., 2025; Busbridge et al., 2025; Lu and Liu, 2026). Caching the teachers top-K logits stores values and indices per token (Ryskulov et al., 2026); streaming avoids it. KD frameworks. Table 2 compares the open frameworks we ran against DisaggKD; all 3 keep teacher and student on the same GPUs in the modes we ran: Megatron-Bridge ModelOpt (NVIDIA, 2025a, 20242026), KDFlow (Zhang et al., 2026), 2 and NeMo-RL (NeMo RL, 2025). Like KDFlow and Maestro (Yuan et al., 2026), we send hidden states instead of logits, but stream the states from teacher replicas by NCCL P2P to every tensorparallel rank of the student under prefetch ring, with vocabulary-sharded loss and memory and traffic models for both placements (3, 4). Disaggregation and fused losses. Separating phases that contend for one device has paid off in LLM serving, with prefill and decode on separate pools (Zhong et al., 2024; Patel et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2025). RLHF systems place the actor, reference, and reward models flexibly (Sheng et al., 2025) and search plans with cost estimator (Mei et al., 2025); we separate the teacher of KD. On the student side, chunked and fused losses avoid materializing the full logits tensor in cross-entropy (Wijmans et al., 2025; Hsu et al., 2025) and in offline KD (Ryskulov et al., 2026).

Loss and its position. Offline distillation stores teacher outputs as generated sequences (Kim and Rush, 2016) or truncated top-K logits (Ryskulov et al., 2026). On-policy distillation (OPD) trains the student on its own samples and matches the teachers token-level distributions on them (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024; Qwen Team, 2025). Our objective (9) is neither. Its loss and λ schedule follow SlimQwen (Tang et al., 2026) without its multi-token-prediction (MTP) terms (SQ-L+K, SlimQwens LM+KD mixture): the fullvocabulary forward KullbackLeibler (KL) divergence between the teachers and the students nexttoken distributions, in its soft cross-entropy form, mixed with the LM loss as (1 λ) LLM + λ LKD and λ decaying from 1 to 0.75, where λ=1 gives the KD-only variant. ModelOpt and KDFlow minimize the same full-vocabulary forward KL, and NeMo-RL takes the KL over the top 8192 columns. ModelOpts loss balancer (Bal-L+K, its LM+KD balancer) rescales the KD term to the LM loss instead of weighting by λ, which gives the KD term gradient weight of 0.89  (Table 21)  . sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: Memory and traffic models predict the colocated memory limits. On Qwen3.5 DisaggKD matches the colocated LM loss and is faster than colocated runs with the same loss, and the fused loss of DisaggKD lets colocated run train on as few nodes at similar or faster speed; DisaggKD is memory efficient when the student spans several nodes. On the larger pairs colocated runs with fused loss still run OOM where DisaggKD trains.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: DisaggKD needs separate teacher nodes, so where colocated layout already fits the pair it uses more GPUs. Each framework runs under its own recipe; aligning hyperparameters across frameworks, isolating the cause of the NaN in the colocated Nemotron student, and fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP) at pp 1 are outside this paper. The estimation models are fitted to the parallelism ranges and sequence lengths we ran, and some of their terms rest on few runs. We study where the teacher runs and how its loss is computed, not how to raise downstream quality; the runs are short, with 2 seeds on 1 pair, on 1 node type and 1 English corpus.

Unlike DisaggKD, which forms the logits window by window from hidden states, this criterion reads the full materialized logits. (3) SQ-L+K fused-W (W: the models (2) with that fusion cross-entropy fusion off): turned off, so that the logged-only cross-entropy takes the unfused vocabulary-parallel path, which normalizes in place on its single fp32 copy of the logits. DisaggKD evaluates no model cross-entropy: its forward step returns the pre-head hidden states, and the loss module computes the LM and KD terms on windows of 1024 to 4096 rows (Appendix C.1), so the fusion option does not apply to it. Colocated-side enablers. Keeping the colocated runs on Megatron-Bridge used 3 enablers: textextracted copy of the Qwen3.5 teacher (the releases vision wrapper cannot ride PP), preconverted sharded checkpoint for the Qwen3-235B teacher, and communicator pre-warming at training start; the converted and extracted teachers were not compared with the originals. Token accounting. Our first KDFlow and NeMoRL inputs held 1 document per sample, and FineWeb-Edu documents average 840 to 900 tokens, so global batch of 128 would hold 0.11M tokens against 4.19M (Qwen3.5) or 0.52M (Qwen332B) for ModelOpt and DisaggKD, which concatenate documents into full-length sequences. We therefore ran KDFlow and NeMo-RL on the corpus packed into samples of the same length (documents concatenated, the remainder dropped; 32,768 tokens for Qwen3.5 and 4096 for Qwen3-32B, except NeMo-RL on Qwen3.5, which ran 4096-token samples), and counted tokens by re-tokenizing the packed samples. KDFlow receives the packed text as response to fixed prompt without chat template, because its 2 chat-template paths disagreed by 2 tokens per sample; its samples render to 32,682 tokens on average on Qwen3.5 (at most 32,723, under its limit of 32,768) and 4026 on Qwen3-32B. NeMo-RLs samples average 4091 tokens. The tokens per step are in Table 19. NeMo-RLs x-token recipe (its off-policy distillation) exports the teachers full-vocabulary logits into persistent per-rank buffer whose size is proportional to the tokens per step on the Qwen3.5 pair: 30 GiB at 1.05M tokens and 121 GiB at 4.19M, which does not fit an 80 GiB GPU beside the models, as 2 failed 4.19M-token runs showed. The step of 1.05M tokens in Table 19 was the largest that ran on Qwen3.5; 4.19M tokens ran OOM and 2.1M was not attempted. KDFlow at 4.18M tokens ran OOM without sleep mode (the students forward, with the teachers weights resident) and without the chunked loss (a teacher-head chunk wanted 15 GiB with 8 GiB free); with sleep mode and chunk of 4096 tokens its device reading is at the limit  (Table 19)  . Systems comparison. Table 19 lists the measured runs behind Table 2. The global batch is 128 for every stack, except the 4-node DisaggKD run and the 3-node fused-W run on Qwen3.5, whose global batch is 126 so that dp=3 divides it, and NeMo-RL on Qwen3.5, whose batch is 256 sequences of 4096 tokens. DisaggKD trains on Qwen3-32B with SQ-L+K on 1 trainer node and 1 producer node of 4 TP2 replicas, so 2 nodes against 1.
